metadata.title: Unlocking mathematical potential through school-based language learning: Insights from PISA 2018

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PISA 2018 microdata for 15-year-old students and applies model-based approaches (linear mixed models and random forest) after filtering to language learners in mainstream programmes. The manuscript reports stratified sampling and complex survey design as part of PISA’s general methodology, but it does not specify whether PISA sampling weights or replicate weights were applied in the authors’ R analyses. Because the Study 2 model is a random forest implemented via the randomForest package, the analysis likely proceeded without native incorporation of PISA sampling weights (tree-based ML models are not inherently weight-aware), and the paper does not report a weight-aware alternative. Analysts using the OECD PISA 2018 database should consider applying the appropriate student sampling weights (and replicate weights if variance estimation is required) when estimating population-representative effects; however, the paper’s reported ML fit metrics should be interpreted as predictive associations within the analytic sample rather than fully design-weighted population estimates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Study 1 analytic sample was restricted to PISA 2018 15-year-old students who were classified as language learners in mainstream programmes where foreign language is taught as a subject (excluding immersion/bilingual contexts). Operationally, inclusion required that the reported home language matched the language of assessment; students with language mismatch were excluded. Additional exclusions removed cases with missing or invalid responses for key variables and removed extreme outliers (including outlier handling for FLMINS via capping/winsorisation and within-school IQR trimming). After these filters, 34% of cases were removed for invalid/incomplete data, 13% for language mismatch, and 4% for outlier removal, yielding 300,656 students across 73 countries/economies for the FLMINS→math association model. Study 2 used the same filtered student sample for the ML model and further incorporated teacher questionnaire data by restricting to language teachers; because only 19 countries administered the teacher questionnaire, the teacher-linked sample comprised 53,459 students and 16,342 teachers.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Mathematics (15-year-olds), Study 1 (main model; PVs pv_math1–pv_math10)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Linear mixed model (LMM): FLMINS coefficient b = 0.08 per minute (≈ b = 4.8 per additional hour/week), p < .001; conditional R2 = 0.865, marginal R2 = 0.162; N CNTSTUID = 300,656; N CNT = 73.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Mathematics (15-year-olds) the study leveraged Foreign language learning time, Mathematics learning time, Socioeconomic status (ESCS), Academic year level, and Multicultural curriculum to model Mathematics achievement (Plausible Values pv_math1–pv_math10), finding that longer exposure to foreign language instruction was associated with a modest but statistically robust increase in mathematics scores (b = 0.08 per minute; ≈ +4.8 points per additional hour/week, p < .001). This indicates that prioritising sustained, school-based foreign language learning—especially when embedded in culturally enriched curricula—may support numeracy outcomes and potentially help reduce equity gaps, though the cross-sectional design prevents causal claims.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Mathematics (15-year-olds), Study 2 (Random Forest; PVs for Math Score)
main_findings.target_variable: Mathematics achievement (Plausible Values for Math Score)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest: OOB R2 = 0.962, RMSE = 17.29, MAE = 9.43; hold-out test R2 = 0.966, RMSE = 17.16, MAE = 9.41; variable importance (%IncMSE): ESCS = 364.9%, FLMINS = 363.3%, MCCUR = 277.9%, MMINS = 274.9%, SCHSIZE = 259.4%; GCSELF %IncMSE = 0%. Robustness: PV3 R2 = 0.962, RMSE = 19.95, MAE = 10.83; removing ESCS/GENDER/GRADE reduced fit to R2 = 0.83, RMSE = 36.92, MAE = 23.73 but FLMINS remained most important.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Mathematics (15-year-olds) the study leveraged Socioeconomic status (ESCS), Foreign language learning time, Multicultural curriculum, Mathematics learning time, and School size in a Random Forest model to predict Mathematics achievement (Plausible Values for Math Score), finding that foreign language learning time was among the strongest predictors and that multicultural curriculum integration was the most prominent programme feature (importance %IncMSE: ESCS 364.9%, FLMINS 363.3%, MCCUR 277.9%). This indicates that policy efforts to improve mathematics outcomes may benefit from investing in high-quality, culturally integrated foreign language programmes, while also recognising that PV conditioning and predictive ML fit inflate performance and do not establish causality.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses OECD PISA 2018 microdata for 15-year-olds to examine whether school-based foreign language (FL) learning is associated with mathematics achievement across 73 countries/economies. In Study 1, a linear mixed model (LMM) predicts mathematics PV scores using FL learning time per week (FLMINS) alongside socioeconomic and contextual controls; FLMINS shows a positive association with mathematics (b = 0.08 per minute; ≈ +4.8 PISA points per additional hour/week, p < .001), with conditional R² = 0.865 and marginal R² = 0.162. In Study 2, a random forest model predicts mathematics PVs using both student and FL programme characteristics; performance is high (OOB R² = 0.962; hold-out R² = 0.966) with low errors (RMSE ≈ 17.2; MAE ≈ 9.4). Variable importance indicates ESCS and FLMINS are top predictors, and multicultural curriculum integration (MCCUR) is the strongest programme feature. Limitations include cross-sectional design (correlation not causation) and the fact that PVs are conditioned on background variables, which can inflate predictive fit.
